steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement at the top of the file to import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the symbols you need from the package name.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have the necessary imports to use React and the useState hook for state management.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing component state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import syntax. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add an import statement at the top of the file that brings in React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main GenericList component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component called GenericList that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax and define an empty props interface.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named GenericList. It should have a return type of JSX.Element and return null. Create an empty interface for props (e.g., interface GenericListProps {}).
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named GenericList is created with an empty props interface and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the GenericList component with TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have: 1) A component named GenericList, 2) An empty props interface, 3) Return type JSX.Element, and 4) It returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't quite right. Check that you've defined a functional component called GenericList with an empty props interface and returns null.

steps.title: Add generic type parameter to GenericList
steps.instruction: Add a generic type parameter T to the GenericList component definition. The component should accept a type parameter T that can be used for the items it will display.
steps.hint: In TypeScript, you can add a generic type parameter after the component name, like GenericList<T>. This allows the component to work with different types of data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The GenericList component should now have a generic type parameter T in its definition, making it ready to accept typed props.
successCriteria: GenericList component has a type parameter T
Component definition includes <T> after the component name
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the generic type parameter T to your GenericList component. This is a fundamental TypeScript concept that allows your component to work with different data types while maintaining type safety.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the generic type parameter might not be fully correct. Make sure you add <T> immediately after the component name in the function signature. The component should still return JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The generic type parameter is missing or incorrect. Remember to add <T> after the component name in the function definition. For example: function GenericList<T>() { ... } or const GenericList = <T,>() => { ... }.

steps.title: Define props interface with generic items array
steps.instruction: Inside the GenericList component, define an interface named 'GenericListProps' with a generic type parameter 'T'. Add a property 'items' of type 'T[]' to this interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: interface GenericListProps<T> { items: T[]; }
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a typed interface that describes the props your GenericList component will accept, with a generic items array property.
successCriteria: The interface should be named 'GenericListProps', have a generic type parameter 'T', and contain a property 'items' of type 'T[]'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a typed props interface with a generic items array. This will allow your component to accept different types of data while maintaining type safety.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the interface 'GenericListProps'? Does it have a generic type parameter 'T'? Does it include an 'items' property of type 'T[]'?
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition isn't quite right. Remember to create an interface named 'GenericListProps' with a generic type parameter 'T', containing a property 'items' of type 'T[]'.

steps.title: Add renderItem prop to props interface
steps.instruction: In the props interface you defined earlier, add a property called 'renderItem' with the type '(item: T) => React.ReactNode'.
steps.hint: Add a new property to your interface definition. The type should be a function that takes an item of type T and returns React.ReactNode.
steps.expectedOutcome: The props interface now includes a renderItem property that accepts a function to render each item.
successCriteria: renderItem property exists in the interface
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the renderItem prop to your interface. This function will allow the GenericList component to render each item in a customizable way.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your interface definition. Make sure you've added a property called 'renderItem' with the exact type '(item: T) => React.ReactNode'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface should have a renderItem property with type (item: T) => React.ReactNode. Check that you've added this property correctly to your existing interface.

steps.title: Destructure props in component parameters
steps.instruction: Update the GenericList component's parameters to destructure the items and renderItem props directly, while maintaining the TypeScript type annotation for the props.
steps.hint: Instead of using (props: GenericListProps<T>), you can destructure directly in the parameter: ({ items, renderItem }: GenericListProps<T>).
steps.expectedOutcome: The component parameters should now destructure items and renderItem directly from the props object, making them available inside the component body.
successCriteria: Use correct TypeScript syntax for destructuring in parameters
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully destructured the items and renderItem props directly in the component parameters. This makes the props more accessible inside the component body.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're destructuring both items and renderItem from the props parameter, and that you're maintaining the GenericListProps<T> type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component parameters should destructure both items and renderItem from the props object. Remember to use TypeScript syntax: ({ items, renderItem }: GenericListProps<T>).

steps.title: Return a wrapper div element
steps.instruction: Inside the GenericList component, replace the current null return statement with a wrapper div element that will contain the list items. The div should have a className of 'list-wrapper'.
steps.hint:
Return JSX by replacing 'return null;' with 'return
;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div element with className 'list-wrapper' instead of null.
successCriteria: The component returns a JSX div element with className 'list-wrapper'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned a wrapper div element from the GenericList component. This provides the container structure we'll use to render our list items.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're returning a div element with className 'list-wrapper'. Make sure you're replacing the null return statement completely.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element with className 'list-wrapper'. Check that you're using JSX syntax and replacing the null return statement.

steps.title: Map over items array to render each item
steps.instruction: Inside the div element, use the map method on the items array to call renderItem for each item. Return the result of the map as JSX content.
steps.hint: Remember that renderItem is a function that takes an item of type T and returns JSX. Use items.map(item => renderItem(item)).
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now render each item from the items array using the renderItem function inside the div wrapper.
successCriteria: The code should include a map method call on items inside the div, calling renderItem for each item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully mapped over the items array and used the renderItem function to render each item. This is the core functionality of your generic list component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the map method on the items array and calling renderItem for each item inside the div.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the div, you need to use items.map(item => renderItem(item)) to render each item from the array.

steps.title: Add key prop to each rendered item
steps.instruction: Inside the map callback, wrap each rendered item in a div element and add a unique key prop using the item's index.
steps.hint: When mapping over an array in React, each element needs a unique key prop. You can use the index parameter from the map callback as the key.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each item in the list will be wrapped in a div element with a unique key prop, satisfying React's list rendering requirements.
successCriteria: Add a div element inside the map callback
Add a key prop to the div
Use the index parameter as the key value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a key prop to each rendered item. This is essential for React to efficiently update lists.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the div wrapper and the key prop using the index parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the map callback, you need to wrap each rendered item in a div element with a key prop.

steps.title: Create a sample User interface
steps.instruction: Create a User interface with id (number), name (string), and email (string) properties. Define this interface above the GenericList component.
steps.hint: Use the TypeScript interface keyword to define a User interface with the specified properties and their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface is defined with three typed properties, ready to be used as a concrete type for the GenericList component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a User interface with proper TypeScript types. This interface will allow you to create type-safe user data for your generic list.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your User interface has all three required properties with the correct TypeScript types: id (number), name (string), and email (string).
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface wasn't properly defined. Remember to use the interface keyword, name it 'User', and include id (number), name (string), and email (string) properties.

steps.title: Initialize sample users state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the GenericList component, initialize a state variable called 'users' using useState. The state should be typed as an array of User objects and initialized with an empty array.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a type parameter to specify the array type. Remember to import useState if not already imported (it is in the code).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing typed state with useState
const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed state variable 'users' ready to hold an array of User objects.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with the type parameter User[] and initial value of an empty array, inside the GenericList component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized a typed state variable for users. This prepares the component to manage a list of User objects.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the state is typed as User[] and initialized with an empty array. Check the syntax of useState with a type parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. Remember to use useState with the type User[] and an empty array as the initial value.
